reason: §176 opens: "Kalid's 'son of the dog' is the same as the much extolled 'son of the philosophers.'" Jung asserts the synonymy directly; claim_type jung-asserts is correct.

§176: "The ambiguity of this figure is thus stressed: it is at once bright as day and dark as night, a perfect coincidentia oppositorum expressing the divine nature of the self." The figure is the filius; direction and claim_type correct.

§176 explicitly quotes the Elenchos of Hippolytus: "For the Logos is a dog who guards and protects the sheep." Quote accurate (ellipsis only spans a Greek bracket); claim_type jung-quotes-source with source named is correct.

§179 says the dog motif is "a necessary counterbalance to the excessively praised 'light-nature' of the stone" — it counterbalances the stone's over-praised light-nature (the dog being the stone's dark aspect), not the lapis as such. Object as stated slightly distorts the claim.

§182 quotes Philaletha's Introitus apertus: "the infant hermaphrodite, who is infected from his very cradle by the bite of the rabid Corascene dog." The hermaphrodite is the rebis; direction, claim_type, and source are correct.

In §182 the antecedent of "his raving madness" is the infant hermaphrodite (the Chamaeleon bitten and maddened by the dog), not the dog; the quote's splice onto "Then will the impatient, swarthy, rabid dog" misleadingly makes the dog the object of assuaging.

§180: "This 'liquid' [the succus lunariae] comes from the unconscious but is not always an authentic content of it." 'Derives-from' matches "comes from"; the qualification concerns authenticity of content, not origin.
§184: "In itself the unconscious is neutral, and its normal function is to compensate the conscious position." Direct assertion, direction correct.

§194 closes: "that 'crude sulphur' which with 'arsenical malignity' prevents man from discovering his true self." Jung applies the sulphur symbol psychologically in his own voice; direction and claim_type correct.
§215 quotes Paracelsus's De pestilitate, whose Latin is glossed "thus the moon in the sky is the eye of the basilisk of heaven." Quote accurate; jung-quotes-source with source named is correct.

§216: "the baying of Hecate is always there, whether it sound from near or from far. This is true of everything feminine and not least of a man's anima." 'Haunts' is a fair paraphrase of the ever-present sinister Hecate aspect of the anima; medium confidence appropriately kept.
§218: "This role of Luna devolves upon the anima, as she personifies the plurality of archetypes." Direct assertion, direction correct.
§220 opens: "From the darkness of the unconscious comes the light of illumination, the albedo." Direct assertion, direction correct.
§223: the moon "is also a giver of light and can therefore represent consciousness," specifically woman's lunar consciousness. The hedged relation 'can-represent' preserves Jung's qualification.
§225 says the inversion of roles "is PROBABLY the chief psychological source for the alchemical concept of the hermaphrodite"; the flat relation drops Jung's hedge and the qualifier 'chief'.

§234: digressions are needed "to do justice to the various aspects of the unconscious that are expressed by salt," and Sal is named an attribute of Luna, who symbolizes the unconscious. Direction (salt expresses aspects of the unconscious) is correct.

§238: "His [the devil's] equivalent in alchemy is the dark side of Mercurius duplex and, as we saw, the active sulphur." The relation correctly restricts the equivalence to Mercurius's dark side rather than equating the devil with Mercurius wholesale.

§238's apposition identifies the extracted spirit in Reusner's Pandora as "the anima mundi who has been freed from the shackles of matter, the filius macrocosmi or Mercurius-Anthropos" — an identification of the anima mundi in its freed state, interpreting one illustration; a flat context-free 'identical-to' overreaches.

correction.subject: anima-mundi
correction.note: Scope: the anima mundi as freed from matter, in Jung's reading of the Pandora extraction illustration.
